title: Ziggurat
text: I've never played a first-person dungeon crawler before, so this game was a new experience for me. Full disclosure: I played this game using a controller. You can use either K&M or Controller, but I prefer using a controller when it's adequately supported. It was definitely a cool experience when I first started. It didn't occur to me until after a handful of attempts that this game feels so familiar because it's essentially playing Binding of Isaac or Legend of Zelda, in the view of Isaac or Zelda. While I don't believe this game has a comparable number of items compared to BoI or LoZ, it nevertheless has a good feel when playing. Much like BoI, it's rogue-like, so each level is randomly-generated, items and stats are reset before each new run, and deaths are permanent. A main difference I see between the playstyle of BoI and Ziggurat is that Ziggurat has a levelling system, where your character can gain experience, and more-or-less can guarantee an upgrade for direct ability. BoI, while guarantees an upgrade at the start of your run, does not guarantee any upgrades beyond the first. Don't forget that this is a rogue-like game, so your level resets after each run. Overall, if you like the Binding of Isaac games, you'll probably like this game.

title: Ziggurat
text: Pretty solid rouge lite fps Ziggurat has you playing an apprentice wizard trying to earn his place among his brothers by taking on a magic tower. you face several randomly generated floors each room offers either a trap, a potential treasure or a wave of enemies.  there are also statues you can pray to and offer health or magic for either a random reward or pentaly. as with most rouge lites the randomness will make or break your run.  your start the game with a wand that is fast and weak with recharging ammo pool and a random secondary weapon in the form of either a spell a staff or an artifact (think magic machine like a grenade or pistol)  you can find more weapons as you explore and at the start of each floor though you can only carry one of each type.  you can level up in the game and each time you get a choice of a number of perks and as you play the game more and more, you unlock more items and perks for future play throughs and can even unlock new characters with there own unique starting stats and ablitities the game is pretty fun.  each weapon slot has its own feel and the different varients of each slot give you alot of play styles to work with.  the  enemies, while not very complex, come in a large variety and each have there own dangers.  and each floor has its own giant size boss.  everything is bright and colorful and the graphics have a world of warcraft feel to them. The game can be beaten in a couple of hours but will likely take you longer due to the random nature of the game and the increassing difficulty plus with all the unlockable content there is pretty high level of difficulty Not a bad game for the price.  Cool concept, solid execution short but replayable.  If you want somthing a bit different give it a look

text: This game is incredible! It reminds me of Heretic or Hexen (the spell using and the level design), but it is random each play.  There are tons of unlockables, from perks to playable characters.  Random bonuses and weapons each playthrough, sort of like the Binding of Isaac.  The game runs great on my laptop with the graphic settings maxed, and it looks fantastic.  The controls are smooth (using a wired Xbox360 controller, but I imagine it controls even better with mouse and keyboard).  The pacing is pretty hectic, but once you clear a room you have time to resituate .  I could easily see this as a retail game.  Also, the game gets updated pretty regularly, with fixes and new content.  Some people might complain that it is short, but they have added an Endless option to difficulty, which I assume means what it says (I have not tried it yet).  This is the best thing I have played in a very long time, and it has plenty of replay value to satify those skeptics who think it might be too short.  As of 3/8/15 it is on sale, and I highly encourage anyone to pick it up.  Even once it isn't on sale, I still think it will be worth it.  I can't wait to see what these developers do next!

title: Ziggurat
text: While I initially had some issues with aiming (I'm still getting used to FPS games where I don't have the option to 'aim down the sights') the simple, yet deep system that the developers created for Ziggurat makes for a very challenging and fun game that I strongly urge people to play. Based on the 'rogue-like' genre of games where each level is generated at random, I've never had a session play in the exact same way at all. The weapons you acquire are randomized, the boss fights at the end of a level are random, and your character perks are offered to you as (usually) the choice between two new perks. Sometimes, this does translate into a game wherein you get your enchanted backside handed to you because the random number generator gods decided that they just don't like you anymore' but the game is short enough on a playthrough that you don't feel like you've invested so much time and effort into being thwarted by bad luck. Furthermore, unlocks ranging from new abilities, perks, characters, and weapons serve to keep you charging at the Ziggurat screaming "Thank you, may I have another?!?!" A well-developed RPG levelling system helps you build your character, unique classes of weapons even further diversified by differences between individual weapons, and a diverse range of enemies (that in later levels are enhanced by various environmental conditions) all blend together to make a very fun, challenging, and rewarding experience.

title: Ziggurat
text: Gah, this game needs a middle option between recommend and not. It's not bad, it's more that its issues are exacerbated by being a roguelite.  Specifically, there's two issues that REALLY bring this game down: 1. The game is balanced around you picking up experience orbs, but doing so is often extremely dangerous, and they disappear too quickly.  This could've been mitigated by simply automatically giving you experience upon killing enemies, or at least making sure the orbs never disappear. 2. Despite this being a projectile based shooter, and not a hitscan one like Wolfenstein or Serious Sam, enemies track you FAR too well, and unless you're playing on Easy, they hit insanely hard.  Some enemies simply aim well, others actually fire homing projectiles, some can fill whole rooms with their poison/fire/etc.  It just feels unfair at times.  It's seriously easier to dodge hitscan shots from zombies in Doom than the projectile weapons here.  And then the game's final boss is just blatantly OP and unfair. The first issue is pretty contentious by any standards (IIRC, Tower of Guns and Kingdom Hearts both have the same issue), but the second is only a problem because this is a roguelite.  Were this a game where you could save normally, you could practice and it might not feel so bad dying to a random hit from seemingly nowhere. In spite of all this, I don't think it's a terrible game... just not one I can easily recommend.  If anything, this is probably the best FPS-roguelite, maybe even the best roguelite involving shooting period (only Binding of Isaac Rebirth, Relic Hunters Zero, and Nuclear Throne would rival it), on the market as of this post.  But the thing is, you're either playing it for the short game on Easy, which is only about 2 - 3 hours of your time, or the long game on any other difficulty, which is pure frustration. If you're ok with such a short game at $14.99 (read, Easy difficulty) then I recommend it. If you love roguelites in general and get pleasant tingles at the thought of a game being blatantly unfair and masochistic (read: any other difficulty besides Easy), then I recommend it. If you get the game on a sale or Humble Bundle, then I recommend it. If you just wanna shoot stuff and don't care about anything else, then I probably recommend it, as you could do a lot worse than this.  I mean, it doesn't have THE best shooting/combat mechanics in the world or anything, but they're pretty fun, especially by roguelite standards. For everyone else?  I probably would not recommend it.

text: This is the more dour Fantasy brother to Tower of Guns - It's a roguelike first person shooter using fantasy elements and weapons, and card based upgrades that only last through your current game (although you can unlock new characters). It is also very intense - I noticed I was dodging attacks in my chair, and holding my breath at the end of some of the later level's battles. Because it's a roguelike, it'll reward returning to it again (and I will, just like Tower of Guns), but I made it through the five levels of the main game and finished off the final boss (barely). The levels are beautiful, the monsters are ugly, and it's challenging but fair. I'm really glad I picked it up; it's definitely worth a try if you liked games like Hexen and Heretic way back when and want something with a similar feel. My only negative is that it doesn't have enough secrets in it, but that's not much of a complaint.

text: Basically the developer 'Quiet River' (no website provided) has loaded a Gatling gun full of achievements and is rapid firing them at you with this game with each click. The objective of the game is to get the blue box on screen to touch a green field. text: A really good visual novel. I'll be honest, despite the number of positive reviews this game has, it took me by surprise. Looking at the stills, and even the trailer, I was kind of expecting a light hearted fantasy romp. Perhaps the next episode does go in that direction, but this one goes elsewhere. Selphine is a rather sheltered princess of a peaceful kingdom, and she and her bodygaurd Ritona are in rather dire straits at the start of the game, with the kindom under attack by unknown forces. In the course of events, both girls are whisked away to a far off land for what I initially took to be going the direction of a basic fish out of water story. While the plot does that to a certain extent, it actually gets far more philosophical than I had any right to expect, dealing with magic vs science and eventually even what it is to be human and what consitutes life and sentience. The story itself is well written and the localization does a really solid job. There is the occasional slightly awkward sentence structure, but nothing that really stands out. It's good work from the translation team, which is needed given the rather heavy subject matter at times. There was one particular moment in the story that felt a little odd, like something had been cut from the story, but the fact that this stands out as unusual speaks to the over all solid story telling as a whole. I'm sorry if I've mostly been dancing around things, but it's really a story I don't want to spoil. Frankly, if you like VN's that are more about characters and world building than wall to wall action, you are probbably going to enjoy yourself with this one. Also, while the game definitely has its laughs, it's not the light hearted romp the screenshots may lead you to expect. While I would have been perfectly happy with that, I was much happier with where it actually went. 8/10

text: I did enjoy the VN. The art is only about average for the talking portraits, but really quite good for the CG images. The story pulls you in and gets you interested at first. The music suits the events on screen. Why the not recommended? There's a section about 2/3's of the way in where the exact same information is repeated around a half dozen times in a row in different stories between different people which feels like the grind padding you get in a lot of RPG's, the kind that's there only to increase the total amount of time played. The twists, aside from the not-so-exciting cliffhanger ending, are so heavily talked about and foreshadowed that only the specifics are kept hidden from the player. And even then the specifics of those specifics, like how did "he" know about this process and specifically how did "he" recreate it other than a Frankenstein's monster type of effect, are never explained well enough at least to my satisfaction, and considering how in-depth the writing goes to ensure the player has a firm enough grasp on the mechanics of mana in this world this is more a little troubling in terms of consistency. In fact my biggest complaint with this VN is how short it is, and how slowly the story moves. Maybe this is just the current state of VN's? I don't dislike the game, I did enjoy playing it, but if I hadn't acquired it in a bundle I know for certain I couldn't have brought myself to buy it. I remember playing games like this 10, 20 years ago with multiple CG's, stories, endings, choices, characters, etc. which could easily last someone a good 10, 20 hours or more, even with a skip option. This game had 1 choice only, and it was pretty obvious what the right answer was, though it seems like the choice doesn't matter. At the pace the story unfolded for this, the first entry, I'm starting to think the developers have no intention of this game series having a real ending after 2, 3, or 4 games, I could easily see them trying to make 10 or more. This is based purely on my experience playing this game. If you absolutely love VN's and really don't like games otherwise, this might be for you. But to me it's too slow, too short, too limited, and far too expensive considering all of those things. Could easily make a pretty good animated series one day; the entire first VN could be summed up in one to three episodes easily, considering internal monologue, seemingly the bulk of the writing, doesn't normally exist in anime. Thanks for reading and have a nice day.

text: Fault Milestone One is a Visual Novel and the first entry in the Fault series. + Excelent story + Likable characters + Good drawings + Good soundtrack + Works with a controller (despite Steam saying it doesn't) + Works on Arch Linux - Some funny small bugs Fault depicts a world where mana exists and is used in almost every aspect of life. The game is linear and 100% story driven so any further details would spoil the game. There is no hentai or ecchi in this game and it's perfectly fine for teenagers despite having some violence. There is only one choice in the entire game and it doesn't really have an impact besides showing an alternative text. The art style and music fit the story perfectly. Other than that there's not much else to point out, you either like the story or you do not. The story at first may feel like it's throwing too much information and getting nowhere but it does get a lot more interesting as it goes on. The characters have very distinct personalities and are very likable and relatable. The story gets very dramatic at some parts but it does leave you feeling that it made sense and perhaps think about the concept itself. There is nothing annoyingly unrealistic. The end will leave wanting more but at that point you can buy Milestone Two. Without spoiling, all I can say is that in my opinion the story is very interesting and worth your time. The game works with all regular devices: keyboard, mouse or controller. There are some minor bugs but nothing special. When you go the pause meny and press down with the D-Pad you don't get the next option, you get the last one. You can still get to the option you want with some left, right, down, up gymnastic. It didn't annoy me at all tbh, it's funny bug. Another one is that it's hard to see whether Yes or No is being chosen but you can still get it right. Also I didn't find a way to quick save with the controller. If you like visual novels this is definitely one game to get.

text: This game is terribly written, and to make matters worse, terribly translated. It’s also incredibly boring. Sekai Project, the localization team, was also responsible for the terrible Clannad translation. Mericifully, this isn’t nearly as unreadable as Clannad was, but it’s still just really, really shoddy work. Not just on the typos and grammatical errors front, but as a localization, it’s full of terrible decisions. Why did they choose to stick so many extra letters into words like “Rughzenhaide” and remove vowels? The original Japanese reads “Ruzenhaido,” which is actually possible to sound out and understand. The translations for the in-game terms are a linguistic cluster♥♥♥♥, and they’re impossible to read or retain because they are full of nonsense character strings that don’t make sense in this language. Why the ♥♥♥♥ would you render “Reinvasta” as “Reighnvhasta”? Just to screw over readers? There’s no other explanation. “Ghnvh” is not a series of characters that should occur sequentially in English. The nadir of this is the localization of the completely normal name “Marie” (マリー) as “Mharie,” which my brain reads as “Maharry,” because that’s not how English ♥♥♥♥ing works. The game itself was terribly constructed, narratively, with long drawn-out worldbuilding explanations right at the beginning, and when you layer the unintelligible place and magic terms on top, it’s just not possible to retain any setting information. It’s not even possible to read or understand it. I honestly couldn’t tell you what any of the place names were; I recognized the words by shape and the letter they started with. This made it almost impossible to stay on top of terms. The result is that often I would find my eyes just glazing over, because the characters would launch into overblowm exposition that essentially took place primarily in a language I didn’t understand. And it’s not like it even mattered. The bulk of the game — the main plot — takes place independent of all the stupid backstory, so it wasn’t even necessary to understand it to follow along. The story itself was bland, but the way it was told was actually fascinating in how terrible it was. This game was apparently originally pitched as an RPG, and it shows — there’s absolutely none of the prosaic narrative crafting here that visual novels require to work. The game begins by dumping tons and tons of irrelevant mechanics and backstory on you, and then it’s always justifying the way people use magic abilities with long, technical explanations, taking breaks even during battle scenes to do this, as though “it’s ♥♥♥♥ing magic” wasn’t enough. It was completely unable to distinguish between necessary and ancillary information, and as a result the pacing is abysmal and the plot is jumbled and confused. It’s impossible to weed out the information that matters to the plot, because the vast majority of it doesn’t. I’ve never wanted to shoot every character in a story with Chekhov’s gun so badly. The pacing issues come to a head in the middle of the game, where one chapter suddenly grinds the plot to a halt to give us a half-hours worth of backstory, and then the very next chapter has a different character give the same exposition to the protagonists. I don’t know what anyone was thinking with this. It’s more than an hour of gameplay, all of which could be cut without taking away anything. Just scene after scene after scene of redundant, unnecessary backstory. As though the writer had to include every random thought that went through their head in the narrative on penalty of death. It was mind-numbing. To make matters worse, the game has a habit of using several screens of “……” as scene breaks, so a significant chunk of the game is essentially flipping through blank pages. It’s literally nothing. (It also doesn’t help that the worldbuilding is complete nonsense even when it’s intelligible… the nonmagical lands don’t have electricity… but they have MRI machines??) The game isn’t long — about four hours — but it feels much longer and it should be much, much shorter. On top of the mountains of extraneous exposition, the writer(s?) also thinks boring day-to-day dialogue is interesting just because it’s happening to their characters. We’re constantly subjected to smalltalk that goes on forever. After a while I just started skipping through it. The whole thing reads like bad fanfic, really.The game constantly falls into the trap of thinking that just because something must have happened, we have to see it.  It seems as though this is the dev’s first VN, and it shows. This was not written by someone who has writing experience. Or someone who is any good at writing. The plot, barebones as it is, is that a kingdom comes under siege suddenly and without warning from the attackers, and the princess and her bodyguard escape, but a magical misfire causes them to be flung to the far reaches of the planet. In a strange land, they have to find their way home, while also learning Life Lessons about love/friendship/shonen from the locals. That’s the frame story. This first episode of the ensuing travelogue revolves around a girl named Rune and her family situation in the first city they come across. The characters range from bland to irritating anime cliches to hiliaribad. The ostensible protagonists, the princess Selphine and her bodyguard Ritona, are inoffensive stock characters — Bubbly Princess and Stoic Bodyguard. Rudo is your typical Alpha Male ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. (Which — it’s interesting, isn’t it, that when you see something like Evil Is Sexy, how it correlates with things like “oh the cruel man who physically threatens you is actually a secret woobie” (is there a name for that trope?)… the game took place in another no-pants-land, but there was something about the Big Bad’s costuming in particular that set off alarm bells for me, and then sure enough, Rudo. All of these tropes are so closely tied together.) The game seemed very proud of itself for managing the most cliche, bare-bones characterization, which is annoying but also kind of funny. And Rune is hilarious. Such an inept writer trying to write a sociopathic character is just amazingly entertaining in the worst way. The faux-business-speak is also hilarious, in a really cringey way. It’s like how a 9-year-old imagines companies are run. In fact, the game was entertaining enough in how bad the writing was that the boringness of it was tolerable. I think my favorite thing was where it tried to claim Rudo invented and owned the stock market. He just owned the whole thing, somehow. And for all the ~female protagoinst~ jargon the dev goes on about, Rudo is obviously the real pet character, and the actual protagonist. Which is irritating. But, more than anything else, this game was incredibly boring. There’s maybe an hour of actual story and necessary dialogue here, so I was often just skipping and skipping through the redundant, irrelevant stuff. The plot underneath it about Rune overall wasn’t bad, but it was so ridiculously, ineptly told. There’s a definite amusement factor in how awful parts of this are, but you absolutely should not pay money for it.
